findings.label: Equivocation
findings.issue: The source infers incoherence from disagreement. The rationale identifies an unsupported inference between two propositions, but no key word whose meaning changes. Recheck whether the exact equivocation definition is met; disagreement does not prove contradiction, but that alone is not equivocation.

findings.label: Argument from ignorance
findings.issue: The locked move challenges the evidential standing of a proposed rival; the frozen critique expressly calls that comparative question legitimate. The rationale must establish an actual claim inferred true solely from nonproof, distinct from the supported imaginary-time equivocation. Under-support of a rival cannot simply be relabeled as a positive creator inference.

findings.label: Confirmation bias
findings.issue: The source distinguishes reports from established events and gives a cumulative argument with an incomplete alternative set. Omission of a legend alternative alone does not establish seeking, interpreting or remembering evidence to favor an existing view while discounting contrary information. Recheck that exact criterion using actual source conduct.

findings.label: Red herring
findings.issue: The ancient-history comparison directly challenges the standard used to reject reported appearance claims. The frozen critique calls it an exaggerated all-or-nothing analogy. Explain why it is actually a diversion to a less relevant issue, rather than an incomplete but direct methodological reply; weak analogy is not automatically a catalog fallacy.

findings.label: Subjective validation
findings.issue: The exact definition requires personal resonance or confirmation of private experience. Citing other people’s private reports without physiological controls does not meet that criterion. The source does not say these reports are persuasive because they personally resonate or confirm the speaker’s own experience. The present acceptance rationale therefore fails the catalog definition.

findings.label: Argument from ignorance
findings.issue: The frozen critique and source identify positive brain-dependence observations and a software analogy. Categorical confidence exceeds that evidence, but the argument is not simply an inference from nonproof. Recheck the absence-of-positive-evidence requirement instead of treating overconfidence as automatic ignorance reasoning.

findings.label: Argument from ignorance
findings.issue: The source offers a substantive but oversimplified evolutionary premise and a counterexample of stranger-directed altruism. It concludes that this account fails; it does not state God as the conclusion of this narrow move. Failure to exclude natural mechanisms is an evidential/inferential gap, not automatically the exact argument-from-ignorance form.

findings.label: Confirmation bias
findings.issue: The source explicitly acknowledges good teachings and evaluates the Golden Rule. The critique identifies absent context and insufficient weighting for the claim most are bad. Recheck whether this establishes the exact confirmation-bias conduct, as opposed to under-supported generalization from chosen examples; do not erase the acknowledged contrary material.

findings.label: Red herring
findings.issue: The rationale/context omit that D’Souza directly answers the hell claim with an emergency-warning analogy and denial that Jesus takes glee. Preserve this qualification. Favorable moral teachings are relevant to Barker’s broad negative appraisal. Any acceptance must identify a distinct irrelevant diversion (such as speculative animus) rather than treating incomplete relevant rebuttal as itself a red herring.
